1.topic: Elizabeth, Zechariah and Mary: the coming of John and Jesus
1.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. narrate the birth and naming of John the Baptist (Luke 1:57-66);
2. describe Mary's visit to Elizabeth and her song of praise (Luke 1:39-56);
3. explain what these events show about God's plan for the coming of Jesus.

## Materials

Bibles, a family chart linking Zechariah, Elizabeth, Mary and Joseph, a writing tablet or slate for the class activity.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: in your language, who gives a baby its name and what does the name usually mean? Take two or three answers, for example Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa naming customs.

## Development

1. Revise Luke 1:5-25: Zechariah's silence. Ask what he was waiting for.
2. Read Luke 1:39-45. Elizabeth's greeting: "Blessed are you among women". Note that the baby leapt in her womb.
3. Read Luke 1:46-56 (the Magnificat). On the board, list what Mary said God has done for the humble, the proud, the hungry and the rich.
4. Read Luke 1:57-66. Discuss why neighbours expected the name Zechariah, and what happened when he wrote the name.
5. Read Luke 1:67-80 briefly: Zechariah's song about John's work to prepare the way.

## Class activity

Pupils write on a slate what Zechariah wrote and then say aloud one line from Mary's song.

## Evaluation

1. Who was Mary's relative that she visited?
2. What happened to Zechariah when he named the baby John?

## Assignment

Write the main ideas of the Magnificat in five short sentences of your own.

reading.title: Two mothers and two sons
reading.content:
# Two mothers and two sons

## Mary visits Elizabeth

After the angel Gabriel told Mary that she would be the mother of Jesus, she travelled quickly to a town in the hill country of Judea to visit her relative **Elizabeth**. As soon as Elizabeth heard Mary's greeting, the baby inside her leapt for joy, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. She said to Mary, "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the child you will bear! ... Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord would fulfil his promises to her!" (Luke 1:39-45). Mary stayed with Elizabeth about three months.

## Mary's song

Mary answered with a song of praise. It is called the **Magnificat**, from the first word in its Latin translation, which means "magnifies". Mary said her soul magnifies the Lord and her spirit rejoices in God her Saviour, because God had looked on her humble state. She sang that God's mercy is for those who fear Him from one generation to the next. God has scattered the proud, brought down rulers from their thrones and lifted up the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty (Luke 1:46-55). The song shows that God cares about the poor and the lowly, and that He keeps His promises to Abraham and his descendants.

## The birth and naming of John

When it was time for Elizabeth's baby to be born, she gave birth to a son. Her neighbours and relatives rejoiced that the Lord had shown her great mercy. On the eighth day, when the baby was to be circumcised and named, the neighbours wanted to call him Zechariah after his father. Elizabeth said, "No! He is to be called John." The people argued that nobody in the family had that name. They made signs to Zechariah to ask what he wanted. He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, "His name is John." At once his mouth was opened and he spoke, praising God (Luke 1:57-64).

Everyone in the area was filled with awe. Zechariah, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied that his son would be called a prophet of the Most High and would go before the Lord to prepare the way for Him (Luke 1:67-79).

## What we learn

- John and Jesus were born by God's plan; John's task was to prepare people for Jesus.
- Obeying God's instruction, even when relatives expect something different, brings blessing. Zechariah and Elizabeth both obeyed the name the angel had given.
- God honours humble people.

2.topic: John's preaching, the early ministry and the first disciples
2.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. state the message John the Baptist preached to the crowds (Luke 3:1-18);
2. explain why Jesus asked to be baptised and what followed (Mark 1:9-13);
3. describe how Jesus called His first disciples and what they gave up (Mark 1:14-20; John 1:35-51);
4. say why the miracle at Cana was called a sign (John 2:1-11).

## Materials

Bibles, a map of Galilee with the Sea of Galilee marked, a small fishing net or a picture of one.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: if a very important visitor was coming to your town, what would the people do to get ready? Link it to John's work of preparing the way.

## Development

1. Read Luke 3:1-14. Write on the board the message to each group: crowds, tax collectors and soldiers.
2. Explain why Jesus was baptised though He had no sin (Matthew 3:15). He identified with His people.
3. Read Mark 1:14-20. The call of Simon, Andrew, James and John. Stress that they left their nets at once.
4. Read John 2:1-11 again. Ask why the Gospel calls the miracle a sign and what it shows about Jesus.

## Class activity

Pupils make a short poster: "Prepare the way", with the three practical instructions John gave.

## Evaluation

1. What did John tell the tax collectors?
2. What did Jesus say He would make of Peter and Andrew?

## Assignment

Write six sentences on what you would be willing to leave behind to follow Jesus.

reading.title: A voice in the wilderness, and four fishermen
reading.content:
# A voice in the wilderness, and four fishermen

## John's message

John the Baptist lived in the wilderness near the Jordan. He wore clothes of camel hair and ate locusts and wild honey. He preached that people must **repent**: turn from their sins and turn to God, and be baptised as a sign of it (Luke 3:1-3). Crowds from Jerusalem, Judea and all the Jordan region went out to him.

John did not flatter the crowds. He told them that being a descendant of Abraham was not enough. They must show by their lives that they had changed: "Produce fruit in keeping with repentance." When the crowd asked what to do, John gave practical answers (Luke 3:10-14).

- To everyone: whoever has two shirts should share with the one who has none, and whoever has food should do the same.
- To tax collectors: collect no more than you are required to.
- To soldiers: do not extort money, do not accuse people falsely, be content with your pay.

John said he baptised with water, but someone more powerful was coming who would baptise with the Holy Spirit. He pointed to Jesus and said, "Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!" (John 1:29).

## Jesus begins his work

After His baptism and temptation, Jesus returned to Galilee and began to preach: "The time has come. The kingdom of God has come near. Repent and believe the good news" (Mark 1:14-15).

## The first disciples

Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw two brothers, Simon (later called Peter) and Andrew, casting a net into the lake. He said, "Follow me, and I will send you out to fish for people." At once they left their nets and followed Him. A little further on, He called James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were mending nets in the boat with their father. They too left their father and the hired men and followed Him (Mark 1:16-20). Later Philip and Nathanael joined them (John 1:43-51).

These first disciples gave up their work, their income and their comfort. They show that following Jesus costs something, but that Jesus gives a bigger work: bringing other people to God.

## The wedding at Cana

Jesus' first miracle, at a wedding at Cana, is called a **sign**. It did more than solve the problem of the wine. It showed Jesus' glory, and His disciples put their faith in Him (John 2:11).

3.topic: The Sermon on the Mount: prayer, love for enemies and the Kingdom
3.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. state how Jesus taught His followers to pray and recite the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:5-15);
2. explain Jesus' command to love enemies (Matthew 5:38-48);
3. relate the Golden Rule and the two gates to life in the Kingdom of God (Matthew 7:12-14).

## Materials

Bibles, a chart with the Lord's Prayer written in phrases, cards marked "Old teaching" and "Jesus' teaching".

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: if someone slaps you in the playground, what do most people want to do? What would a person who follows Jesus do? Take answers without judging.

## Development

1. Read Matthew 6:5-8. Jesus warned against praying to be seen and against empty words. Ask what He said about praying in secret.
2. Break the Lord's Prayer into six phrases and explain each (Matthew 6:9-13). Note that the first three are about God and the last three about us.
3. Read Matthew 6:14-15 on forgiveness.
4. Read Matthew 5:38-48 and set out "You have heard... but I tell you" on cards. Discuss turning the other cheek and going the second mile.
5. Read Matthew 7:12 (the Golden Rule) and 7:13-14 (the narrow gate).

## Class activity

In pairs, pupils role-play a pupil who has been wronged and show a Christian way to respond.

## Evaluation

1. What did Jesus say about people who pray only to be seen?
2. Why should we love our enemies, according to Matthew 5:45?

## Assignment

Write the Lord's Prayer in your notebook and explain one line in your own words.

reading.title: How to pray, and how to treat an enemy
reading.content:
# How to pray, and how to treat an enemy

## How to pray

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus gave three rules about prayer (Matthew 6:5-8).

1. **Do not pray to be seen.** The hypocrites loved to pray on street corners so that people would admire them. Jesus said to go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father in secret, and He will reward you.
2. **Do not babble.** The pagans think they will be heard because of many words. Your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.
3. **Pray simply.** Jesus then gave a model prayer, the **Lord's Prayer** (Matthew 6:9-13):

- "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name": we honour God as holy.
- "Your kingdom come, your will be done": we ask for God's rule on earth.
- "Give us today our daily bread": we ask for what we need today.
- "Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors": we ask for forgiveness and promise to forgive.
- "Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one": we ask for protection.

Jesus added that if we forgive others, our Father will forgive us. If we do not, He will not forgive us (Matthew 6:14-15).

## Love your enemies

In Matthew 5:38-48 Jesus compared the old teaching with His own. People had heard "an eye for an eye", which limited revenge to the same harm. Jesus said, "Do not resist an evil person. If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to them the other cheek also." If a soldier forces you to carry his load one mile, go with him two. People had heard "love your neighbour and hate your enemy". Jesus said, "Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you."

The reason is that this is how God acts. He causes the sun to rise on the evil and the good and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous. If we love only those who love us, we are no different from tax collectors and pagans. Jesus finished: "Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect."

## The Golden Rule and the narrow gate

Jesus said, "In everything, do to others what you would have them do to you" (Matthew 7:12). He also said that the gate to life is narrow and the road is hard, and few find it. The wide gate and broad road lead to destruction, and many go through it (Matthew 7:13-14).

## Lessons

- Real prayer is sincere, simple and often private.
- Christians answer wrong with goodness, not revenge.
- The Kingdom of God asks for a changed heart, not only outward religion.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. say what a parable is and why Jesus taught in parables;
2. tell the parables of the sower, the good Samaritan and the prodigal son;
3. apply the lessons of the parables to everyday Christian living.

## Materials

Bibles, pictures of a farmer sowing seed on a path, rocky ground, thorns and good soil, a road map of Jerusalem to Jericho.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask pupils to tell a short story from their own culture that teaches a lesson, such as a tortoise tale. Ask: why do we remember stories longer than rules?

## Development

1. Define a parable: an earthly story with a heavenly meaning. Read Mark 4:1-20 (the sower) and match the four soils with four kinds of listeners.
2. Read Luke 10:25-37 (the good Samaritan). Note why the priest and Levite passed by, and who the neighbour turned out to be.
3. Read Luke 15:11-32 (the prodigal son). Pupils list the steps: asking for the inheritance, wasting it, coming to himself, the father's welcome, the elder brother.
4. Draw out the teaching of each parable.

## Class activity

In groups, pupils retell one parable in a modern Nigerian setting (for example a traveller robbed on the Lagos-Ibadan expressway) and state its lesson.

## Evaluation

1. In the parable of the sower, what do the thorns stand for?
2. Who was the neighbour in the parable of the good Samaritan?

## Assignment

Write six sentences on how you can be a good neighbour this week.

reading.title: Stories that teach
reading.content:
# Stories that teach

A **parable** is a short story from everyday life that carries a spiritual meaning. Jesus used parables because people remember stories, and because the stories made those who truly wanted to understand think carefully (Mark 4:10-12).

## The sower (Mark 4:1-20)

A farmer went out to sow seed. Some fell on the path, and birds ate it. Some fell on rocky ground, sprang up quickly, but withered in the sun because it had no root. Some fell among thorns, which choked it. Some fell on good soil and produced a crop, thirty, sixty or a hundred times what was sown.

Jesus explained: the seed is the word of God. The path stands for people who hear but Satan takes the word away. The rocky ground stands for people who receive the word with joy but give up when trouble comes. The thorns stand for the worries of life and the love of wealth, which choke the word. The good soil stands for those who hear the word, accept it and produce a crop.

## The good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37)

A teacher of the law asked Jesus, "Who is my neighbour?" Jesus told of a man travelling from Jerusalem to Jericho who was attacked by robbers, stripped, beaten and left half dead. A priest saw him and passed by on the other side. A Levite did the same. But a Samaritan, whom Jews despised, took pity. He bandaged his wounds, put him on his own donkey, took him to an inn and paid the innkeeper to look after him. Jesus asked which of the three was a neighbour to the man. The teacher answered, "The one who had mercy on him." Jesus said, "Go and do likewise."

**Lesson:** our neighbour is anyone in need, whatever his tribe or religion, and love is shown in action.

## The prodigal son (Luke 15:11-32)

A younger son asked his father for his share of the property, travelled to a far country and wasted it all. When a famine came, he took a job feeding pigs and wished to eat their food. He "came to his senses", decided to go home and say, "Father, I have sinned." While he was still a long way off, his father saw him, ran to him, embraced him and gave him a robe, a ring and sandals, and a feast. The elder brother was angry at the welcome, but his father said they had to celebrate because "this brother of yours was dead and is alive again".

**Lesson:** God welcomes sinners who repent, and we should do the same.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. define a miracle and name the different kinds Jesus performed (nature, healing, raising the dead, feeding);
2. narrate the feeding of the five thousand and the calming of the storm;
3. explain what the miracles show about the power and compassion of Jesus.

## Materials

Bibles, five loaves (or bread rolls) and two dried fish for display, a picture of a boat in a storm, a table with columns "Miracle", "Where recorded", "What it shows".

## Starter (5 minutes)

Show five small loaves and ask: could this feed a crowd of five thousand? Take a few answers, then say that today's story begins with this much food.

## Development

1. Define a miracle: an event that cannot be explained by natural laws and that shows God's power. Give the four types and one example of each.
2. Read John 6:1-14. Ask who supplied the food, what Jesus did with it and how many baskets were left.
3. Read Mark 4:35-41. Ask why the disciples woke Jesus, what He said to the wind and what He said to them.
4. Briefly retell the healing of the ten lepers (Luke 17:11-19) and the raising of Jairus's daughter (Mark 5:21-43).
5. Complete the table together.

## Class activity

In groups, pupils choose one miracle and write one sentence on what it shows about Jesus.

## Evaluation

1. Who gave Jesus the five loaves and two fish?
2. How many of the ten lepers returned to thank Jesus?

## Assignment

Write six sentences on how you can show compassion to someone in need this week.

reading.title: Power and compassion
reading.content:
# Power and compassion

A **miracle** is a wonderful event that cannot be explained by natural laws, and that shows the power of God at work. The Gospels record many miracles of Jesus. They fall into four kinds:

- **Healing:** Jesus healed the blind, the lame, the deaf, lepers and the sick.
- **Nature miracles:** He calmed a storm, walked on water, turned water into wine.
- **Feeding miracles:** He fed five thousand and four thousand people.
- **Raising the dead:** Jairus's daughter, the widow's son at Nain, and Lazarus.

## Feeding the five thousand (John 6:1-14)

A large crowd followed Jesus to a hillside near the Sea of Galilee. It was late, and there was no food to buy. Andrew told Jesus about a boy who had five small barley loaves and two small fish, and asked how far they would go among so many. Jesus told the disciples to make the people sit down in groups on the grass. He took the loaves, gave thanks and handed them out to those seated, and did the same with the fish. All ate as much as they wanted. When the people were full, Jesus asked the disciples to collect the leftovers so that nothing was wasted. They filled twelve baskets. The crowd said, "Surely this is the Prophet who is to come into the world."

This miracle shows Jesus' compassion for hungry people, and His power. It also shows that God can use even a small gift when it is given to Him.

## Calming the storm (Mark 4:35-41)

One evening Jesus told His disciples to cross the lake. A fierce storm came up, and waves broke over the boat so that it was nearly swamped. Jesus was asleep on a cushion at the back of the boat. The frightened disciples woke Him and said, "Teacher, don't you care if we drown?" Jesus stood up, rebuked the wind and said to the waves, "Quiet! Be still!" The wind died down and it was completely calm. He then asked the disciples, "Why are you so afraid? Do you still have no faith?" They were terrified and asked, "Who is this? Even the wind and the waves obey Him!"

This miracle shows that Jesus has power over nature and that we can trust Him in our own storms.

## The ten lepers (Luke 17:11-19)

Ten men with leprosy called out to Jesus for mercy. He told them to go and show themselves to the priests, and as they went they were healed. Only one, a Samaritan, came back to thank Jesus and praise God. Jesus asked where the other nine were. This miracle teaches gratitude.

reading.title: The last week
reading.content:
# The last week

The last week of Jesus' life before His death is called **Holy Week**. The Gospels give more space to it than to any other part of His ministry.

## The triumphal entry

Jesus and His disciples came near Jerusalem. He sent two disciples to a village to bring a donkey colt that no one had ridden. People spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the fields and spread them. Those who went ahead and those who followed shouted, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!" (Mark 11:1-10). Jesus rode in on a donkey, not a war horse. This showed that He came humbly, as a king of peace, in fulfilment of Zechariah 9:9. This event is remembered as **Palm Sunday**.

Jesus then went into the temple and drove out those who were buying and selling, saying that God's house should be a house of prayer for all nations (Mark 11:15-17).

## The Last Supper

The chief priests were looking for a way to arrest Jesus quietly. Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, agreed to hand Him over for thirty pieces of silver (Luke 22:3-6; Matthew 26:15). On the evening of the Passover, Jesus sat down to eat with His twelve disciples. He took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said, "This is my body given for you; do this in remembrance of me." After supper He took the cup and said, "This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you" (Luke 22:19-20). He also said that one of them would betray Him. This meal is the origin of Holy Communion, or the Lord's Supper.

## Gethsemane, arrest and trial

After supper Jesus went to the Garden of Gethsemane and prayed, "Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; yet not my will, but yours be done." While He was still speaking, Judas arrived with a crowd, and betrayed Him with a kiss. Jesus was arrested. Peter followed Him to the courtyard of the high priest and denied three times that he knew Him. When the cock crowed, Peter remembered Jesus' words and wept (Luke 22:39-62).

Jesus was tried by the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council, who accused Him of blasphemy. He was taken to Pilate, the Roman governor, who found no basis for a charge, then to Herod, and back to Pilate. Under pressure from the crowd, Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified (Luke 22:66 to 23:25).

## The crucifixion

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. narrate the crucifixion and burial of Jesus (Luke 23:33-56; John 19:38-42);
2. narrate the discovery of the empty tomb and the appearances of the risen Jesus (Luke 24:1-35; John 20:11-18);

Bibles, a picture of an empty tomb with a stone rolled away, a chart of "Friday, Saturday, Sunday".

## Development

1. Read Luke 23:33-49. Discuss the words from the cross and the two criminals. Why did the centurion say Jesus was innocent?
2. Read John 19:38-42 and Luke 23:50-56. Joseph of Arimathea, Nicodemus and the women. Note the tomb, the spices and the Sabbath.
3. Read Luke 24:1-12 and John 20:1-18. The women, the stone, the angels, Mary Magdalene meeting Jesus.
4. Read Luke 24:13-35 (the road to Emmaus). Ask when the two disciples recognised Jesus.
5. Summarise: the tomb was empty, Jesus appeared, and the disciples were changed.

## Class activity

Pupils fill the three-day chart with the events of Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

## Evaluation

1. Who asked Pilate for the body of Jesus?
2. Who was the first person to see the risen Jesus, according to John 20?

## Assignment

Write six sentences on what the resurrection means to Christians.

reading.title: Friday, Saturday, Sunday
reading.content:
# Friday, Saturday, Sunday

## The crucifixion

On Friday Jesus was led to Golgotha, nailed to a cross and crucified between two criminals. Above Him was written, "This is the King of the Jews." The soldiers divided His clothes by casting lots. Jesus prayed, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." One of the criminals mocked Him, but the other said, "Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom," and Jesus answered, "Today you will be with me in paradise." At noon darkness came over the whole land for three hours. Then Jesus cried out and died. The Roman centurion who stood watching praised God and said, "Surely this was a righteous man" (Luke 23:33-47).

## The burial

A good man named **Joseph of Arimathea**, a member of the Jewish council who had not agreed to the plan to kill Jesus, went to Pilate and asked for the body. With Nicodemus, he wrapped it in linen cloth with spices and laid it in a new tomb cut from rock, in which no one had yet been laid. A large stone was rolled across the entrance. It was almost the Sabbath, so the women who had followed Jesus from Galilee saw where He was laid, and went home to prepare spices (Luke 23:50-56; John 19:38-42). The chief priests also asked Pilate to put a guard on the tomb.

## The resurrection

Very early on Sunday, the first day of the week, the women brought the spices to the tomb. They found the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. Two angels asked them, "Why do you look for the living among the dead? He is not here; he has risen!" (Luke 24:1-6). Mary Magdalene stood weeping outside the tomb. Jesus spoke to her, and she recognised Him when He said her name. He told her to tell the disciples (John 20:11-18).

That same day, Jesus joined two disciples walking to Emmaus. They did not recognise Him until He broke bread with them, and then He disappeared. They hurried back to Jerusalem and found the disciples saying, "It is true! The Lord has risen" (Luke 24:13-35). Jesus then appeared to the disciples, showed them His hands and side, and ate with them.

## Why it matters

The resurrection shows that Jesus is the Son of God and that He has conquered sin and death. It gives Christians the hope that those who believe in Him will also rise. It also changed frightened disciples into bold witnesses.

reading.title: Sent to all nations
reading.content:
# Sent to all nations

## The Great Commission

After His resurrection, Jesus met His eleven disciples on a mountain in Galilee. Some worshipped Him, though some doubted. He said, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age" (Matthew 28:16-20). This is called the **Great Commission**. It contains four parts: go, make disciples, baptise and teach. It also contains a promise: Jesus will be with His followers always.

## The ascension

For forty days after the resurrection, Jesus appeared to His disciples and taught them about the kingdom of God. He told them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for the gift the Father had promised, the Holy Spirit. He said, "You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth." Then He was taken up into a cloud, and they could no longer see Him. Two angels told the disciples that Jesus would return in the same way (Acts 1:1-11).

## Pentecost

**Pentecost** is a Jewish festival held fifty days after the Passover. Jerusalem was full of visitors from many nations. The followers of Jesus, about 120 in number, were praying together in one place. Suddenly there was a sound like a violent wind from heaven that filled the house. They saw what looked like tongues of fire resting on each of them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages as the Spirit gave them ability (Acts 2:1-4).

A crowd gathered. Each person heard the believers speaking in his own language about the wonders of God. Some were amazed. Others mocked and said the believers were drunk.

Peter stood up with the eleven and said they were not drunk, since it was only nine in the morning. He explained that this was what the prophet Joel had promised. He preached that Jesus of Nazareth, whom they had crucified, God had raised from the dead. The crowd was deeply moved and asked what to do. Peter said, "Repent and be baptised, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit." About three thousand people were baptised that day (Acts 2:14-41).

## Why it matters

The Holy Spirit gave the disciples power and courage. Visitors who believed took the gospel back to their own countries. The church had begun.

10.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. state what Paul says to children and parents in Ephesians 6:1-4;
2. state what Paul says to wives, husbands, children and fathers in Colossians 3:18-21;
3. apply these teachings to a Nigerian family.

## Materials

Bibles, a chart with columns for "Father", "Mother", "Children", cards with family situations written on them.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: who are the members of a family and what does each one do at home? Take answers about parents, elders and children, and write them under the right headings.

## Development

1. Explain that Paul wrote Ephesians and Colossians to churches, and that he gives instructions for family life.
2. Read Ephesians 6:1-4. Note the command to children, the reason and the promise attached to the fifth commandment. Note the instruction to fathers.
3. Read Colossians 3:18-21. List who is addressed and what each is told.
4. Discuss why Paul adds "in the Lord" and "do not embitter".
5. Show cards with situations; pupils say what the passage teaches in each.

## Class activity

In groups, pupils choose one family situation and write what each member should do according to Paul.

## Evaluation

1. What reason does Paul give for children to obey their parents?
2. What does Paul tell fathers not to do?

## Assignment

Write six sentences on how you help to keep peace in your home.

reading.title: Paul's advice for the home
reading.content:
# Paul's advice for the home

Paul wrote letters to the churches, and in several of them he gave advice on how Christians should live at home. Two of the best known are in Ephesians 6 and Colossians 3.

## Children and parents (Ephesians 6:1-4)

"Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right." Paul gives three reasons why. It is right in itself. It is part of the fifth of the Ten Commandments, "Honour your father and mother". And it is "the first commandment with a promise": that it may go well with you and that you may enjoy long life on the earth. "In the Lord" means that the obedience is shown in a way that pleases Him.

Paul also speaks to fathers: "Do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord." A father must not make his children angry through harshness or unfair treatment. He should teach them well and lead them in the ways of God.

## The household (Colossians 3:18-21)

- **Wives**, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
- **Husbands**, love your wives and do not be harsh with them.
- **Children**, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.
- **Fathers**, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged.

Each member of the family is given a duty, and none of the duties is one-sided. Wives submit, but husbands must love and be gentle. Children obey, but fathers must not provoke them. The family works well when each member does his or her own part out of love for God.

## Why it matters

In Nigerian culture, respect for parents and elders is highly valued. Paul's teaching supports this and adds that parents also have a duty: to treat their children fairly and bring them up well. A home where each person does their part is peaceful, and it becomes a good training ground for life in the church and in society.

## Examples

- A child who runs errands without being asked more than once is obeying "in the Lord".
- A father who explains a decision and does not shout is training, not provoking.
- A husband who helps with household duties is showing love and consideration.
